meta.description: Not MacArthur: the line is from Frank Crane's 1914 essay "Youth." MacArthur kept a framed copy and recited it in 1955; Ullman's family also claimed it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You are as young as your faith, as old as your doubt; as young as your self-confidence, as old as your fear; as young as your hope, as old as your despair'?
meta.ogDescription: MacArthur recited it, but didn't write it: the sentence was printed under Frank Crane's byline in 1914, years before it hung on MacArthur's wall.

answer.label: Not Douglas MacArthur — actually Frank Crane
answer.sourceLine: The sentence comes from Dr. Frank Crane’s essay “Youth,” which was in print by April 1914 and was reprinted under his byline in Cosmopolitan that May. MacArthur kept a framed version of the essay over his desk and recited this passage at his 75th-birthday banquet in 1955, and that is how his name became attached to it. Samuel Ullman’s family also claimed the essay, but Quote Investigator gives Crane’s printings precedence.

source.heading: The documented source
source.excerpt: Whether sixty or sixteen, there is in every human being’s heart the lure of wonder, the sweet amazement at the stars and at starlike things and thoughts, the undaunted challenge of events, the unfailing, childlike appetite for what next, and the joy of the game of living. You are as young as your faith, as old as your doubt; as young as your self-confidence, as old as your fear; as young as your hope, as old as your despair. In the central place of your heart is an evergreen tree; its name is Love. So long as it flourishes you are young. When it dies you are old.
trail: April 1914: the earliest match located by Quote Investigator is Dr. Frank Crane’s essay “Youth” in a Carlsbad, New Mexico newspaper. QI concludes that Crane originated the essay by 1914 (Quote Investigator ↗).
May 1914: Cosmopolitan reprints “Youth” under the byline “By Dr. Frank Crane.” The faith/doubt sentence appears in it word for word (Internet Archive scan ↗).

December 1945: The Reader’s Digest describes a framed version of the essay hanging over General MacArthur’s desk at his Manila headquarters, credited to Samuel Ullman (reported by Quote Investigator ↗).

1955: MacArthur recites the passage, including this sentence, in his main address at his 75th-birthday banquet at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles. TIME prints it as “vintage MacArthur oratory” and does not name a source (TIME, 7 Feb 1955 ↗).

author.name: Frank Crane
author.heading: About the real author
author.bio: Dr. Frank Crane was an American clergyman and popular writer. From 1909 he wrote syndicated newspaper columns and short inspirational essays. His 1921 column “Just for Today” was later adapted, usually without credit, by twelve-step groups. His essay “Youth” travelled the same way: it was reprinted in many periodicals, often without his name, and later credited to Samuel Ullman and to Douglas MacArthur.

misattribution.heading: Why it gets credited to the wrong people
misattribution.intro: This passage has been credited to at least three people besides the writer it was first printed under. MacArthur is the most famous of them.

items.why: MacArthur kept a framed version of the “Youth” essay over his desk, a fact The Reader’s Digest publicized in 1945 (Quote Investigator ↗). He also recited this sentence in his 75th-birthday address, which TIME printed as his own oratory without naming a source (TIME, 1955 ↗). In 1977 an Ann Landers reader declared that the essay “was written by Gen. Douglas MacArthur” (QI). He spoke the words, but he did not write them.

Ullman’s family privately printed a version of the essay in 1920, and a 1934 anthology, The Silver Treasury, credited it to him. Quote Investigator notes that Crane’s essay was circulating by 1914 and gives Crane’s citations precedence (QI ↗). Wikiquote’s main text of Ullman’s “Youth” does not contain this sentence. It lists the sentence only as a variant found in The Silver Treasury (1934) version (Wikiquote ↗).

B. C. Forbes’s 1937 Thoughts on the Business of Life credited a condensed version to Phelan. In that version the sentence is reworded as “You are as old as your doubt, your fear, your despair” (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The exact sentence was in print under Dr. Frank Crane’s byline in 1914, in his essay “Youth” (Cosmopolitan, May 1914 ↗; Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why this one stuck to MacArthur
lead: “Youth” was a short inspirational essay that American periodicals reprinted many times after 1914, often without a byline (Quote Investigator ↗). Its most famous reader was Douglas MacArthur. Wikipedia notes that he hung a framed version of the poem, credited to Ullman, in his Tokyo office and often drew on it in public remarks. As a result the poem became better known in Japan than in the United States (Wikipedia ↗).

When MacArthur recited the passage at his 75th-birthday banquet, TIME headlined its piece “As Young As Your Faith” and presented the words as his own oratory (TIME ↗). An unattributed recitation by a famous general is how a columnist’s line came to be quoted as a soldier’s creed.
context.detailsSummary: Is this line in Ullman’s poem at all?
detailsBody: It depends on the version. The text of Ullman’s “Youth” that Wikiquote gives as its main text goes from “the joy of the game of living” straight to the “wireless station” image, without this sentence. Wikiquote records the faith/doubt sentence as a variant, found in the version printed in Jane Manner’s The Silver Treasury (1934) (Wikiquote ↗).
Crane’s 1914 essay contains the sentence in exactly the wording that circulates today, in the same place: after “the joy of the game of living” and before the heart images (Cosmopolitan, May 1914 ↗).

sourcesVerified.claim: QI's earliest match is Dr. Frank Crane's essay 'Youth' in a Carlsbad, New Mexico newspaper in April 1914 (footnote: Carlsbad Argus, 17 April 1914, p. 8). The essay contains the exact faith/doubt sentence, and QI concludes that Crane originated it by 1914.

QI reports the 1945 Reader's Digest account of a framed version over MacArthur's desk at his Manila HQ, credited to Samuel Ullman; the 1977 Ann Landers reader who said MacArthur wrote it; the 1937 Forbes condensed version credited to L. F. Phelan; the 1920 private printing by the Ullman family; and the 1934 Silver Treasury credit to Ullman.

Cosmopolitan, May 1914 (vol. 56, no. 6) prints 'Youth' under the byline 'By Dr. Frank Crane'. It contains the exact sentence 'You are as young as your faith, as old as your doubt; as young as your self-confidence, as old as your fear; as young as your hope, as old as your despair.' The contents index lists it at p. 721. Confirmed via the item's OCR text file.
The OCR text of the same Cosmopolitan May 1914 item contains the sentence verbatim under Crane's byline.

TIME, 7 Feb 1955, 'OPINION: As Young As Your Faith' (page 2): at his 75th-birthday banquet at the Ambassador Hotel, MacArthur's main address included the passage with the exact sentence. TIME calls it 'vintage MacArthur oratory' and names no source.
Wikiquote's Samuel Ullman page: the main text of 'Youth' lacks the sentence. It is listed only as a Variant, found in the version in The Silver Treasury (1934), edited by Jane Manner, p. 323.
Wikipedia: MacArthur hung a framed copy of a version of Ullman's 'Youth' in his Tokyo office and often drew on it; the poem became better known in Japan than in the US.

Wikipedia: Frank Crane (May 12, 1861 – November 5, 1928), American clergyman and popular writer, wrote syndicated newspaper columns from 1909; his 1921 'Just for Today' was adapted by twelve-step groups.
